## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This case study shows why conformal battery SOH benchmark results should be audited before being treated as reliability evidence. In the corrected real-data analyses, recent-label access produces large but task-dependent method-matched coverage changes. The as-used schema bundle changes coverage in two tasks and increases LNAS false acceptance at one corrected threshold, but it jointly changes multiple columns and the endpoint-wide independent-control gate fails, blocking attribution to bookkeeping fields.

The contribution is therefore a bounded measurement-validity warning: conformal SOH intervals may be useful, but their serviceability interpretation depends on the benchmark-integrity discipline developed and discussed above. Future work should apply this audit to broader field data and prospective forecasting settings.

The implication for reliability engineering is simple: coverage must not be promoted to deployment reliability until the benchmark's information set, split integrity, controls, and decision consequences survive the same audit.

## Data Availability {.unnumbered}

This study uses real cycle-level SOH records from three public battery datasets: the CALCE Battery Research Group battery data repository [@calce_battery_data], the NASA Ames Prognostics Data Repository [@nasa_pcoe_battery_data], and the Oxford Battery Degradation Dataset [@howey2017oxford], all accessed 2026-06-02. The versioned derived-data package, source-data provenance, split manifests, and run manifests underlying every reported value are publicly available in the project replication repository at https://github.com/QuantDiviner/NEX-CP-conformal-soh-audit.

## Code Availability {.unnumbered}

The complete analysis code, locked dependencies, and run manifests are publicly available at https://github.com/QuantDiviner/NEX-CP-conformal-soh-audit. The repository regenerates the scripted results table from which all manuscript values are drawn.
